type: manner — only in the fixed phrase *taken aback*
position: end — right after *taken*
modifies: the passive *be taken* in *be taken aback*

senses.gloss: Surprised and briefly thrown off balance, in *be taken aback*.
examples: I was taken *aback* by how rude he was.
She seemed a little taken *aback* when I mentioned the price.
We were all taken *aback* by the news.

position: end — or before its word (*abjectly poor*)
modifies: verbs of apologizing and failing; adjectives like *poor*

senses.gloss: In a humble, ashamed way.
examples: He apologized *abjectly* for the mistake.
She begged *abjectly* for one more chance.

senses.gloss: Completely and hopelessly, of failure or poverty.
examples: The plan failed *abjectly*.
Many families there live in *abjectly* poor conditions.

position: end — or mid, before a participle (*ably assisted*)

senses.gloss: With skill; competently.
examples: The team was *ably* led by a young captain.
She handled the reporters' questions *ably*.
He was *ably* assisted by two graduate students.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*abnormally high*); end with verbs

senses.gloss: In a way that is not normal or usual.
examples: Her blood pressure was *abnormally* high.
It's been an *abnormally* warm winter.
The cells were growing *abnormally*.

position: end — or before its word (*abominably rude*)
modifies: verbs of behaving and treating; adjectives

senses.gloss: Very badly, in a shocking or offensive way.
examples: The workers were treated *abominably* by the new owners.
He behaved *abominably* at his sister's wedding.
The hotel staff were *abominably* rude to us.

position: before its word — before numbers and amounts, and before *ready*, *done*, *finished*
modifies: numbers, amounts and times; adjectives like *ready* and *done*
contrast: Before a noun, *about* is usually a preposition meaning 'о, про' (*a book about dogs*), and *be about to* means 'вот-вот, собираться'. For 'here and there' Americans say *around* (*walk around*) where British English says *walk about*.

senses.gloss: Approximately; a little more or less than.
examples: The drive takes *about* three hours.
There were *about* fifty people at the party.
I'll be there at *about* six.

senses.gloss: Almost; nearly, often in *just about*.
examples: I'm *about* ready to leave.
We're just *about* done with the kitchen.
He's *about* the only person who knows the password.

ru: в ряд, бок о бок; в курсе
type: place; also manner in *keep abreast of*
position: end
modifies: verbs of moving and standing; *keep* and *stay* + *of*

senses.gloss: Side by side, facing the same way.
examples: The path was too narrow to walk two *abreast*.
Three police cars drove *abreast* down the highway.

senses.gloss: Up to date with news or developments, in *keep abreast of* or *stay abreast of*.
examples: I read the news every morning to keep *abreast* of what's happening.
Doctors have to stay *abreast* of new research.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Suddenly and unexpectedly; also in a short, curt way.
examples: The car stopped *abruptly*.
The meeting ended *abruptly* when the fire alarm went off.
“I have to go,” she said *abruptly*, and hung up.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Without paying attention to what you are doing.
examples: He nodded *absently*, still looking at his phone.
She *absently* stirred her coffee.
“Sure, sure,” he said *absently*.

position: mid or end

senses.gloss: Forgetfully, because your mind is on something else.
examples: I *absentmindedly* left my keys in the fridge.
She was *absentmindedly* twisting her ring.
He walked out *absentmindedly* without paying.

position: end

senses.gloss: In terms of general ideas rather than real examples.
examples: It's hard for young children to think *abstractly*.
He talked *abstractly* about justice but never gave an example.
The problem gets easier once you stop thinking about it so *abstractly*.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*absurdly expensive*); end with verbs

senses.gloss: To a ridiculous degree; in a ridiculous way.
examples: Rent in this city is *absurdly* high.
The instructions were *absurdly* complicated.
He was dressed *absurdly* for a funeral.

position: before its word — mostly in *abundantly clear*; end in the 'plentifully' sense
modifies: adjectives like *clear* and *obvious*; verbs of growing and supplying

senses.gloss: Very; completely, mostly in *abundantly clear*.
examples: She made it *abundantly* clear that she wasn't interested.
It's *abundantly* obvious that the plan won't work.

senses.gloss: In large amounts; plentifully.
examples: Wildflowers grow *abundantly* in these hills.
The region is *abundantly* supplied with fresh water.

position: end

senses.gloss: In an insulting or cruel way.
examples: The fan was thrown out for shouting *abusively* at the referee.
Neighbors said he had treated the dog *abusively* for years.
She reported a customer who spoke to her *abusively*.

position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs (*played abysmally*)

senses.gloss: Extremely badly; to a terrible degree.
examples: The team played *abysmally* in the second half.
Pay for teachers there is *abysmally* low.
The service was *abysmally* slow.

type: viewpoint — 'as far as studies are concerned'
position: before its word — before adjectives (*academically gifted*); end with verbs; front with a comma
modifies: adjectives, participles, verbs, and whole sentences

senses.gloss: In terms of school, studies or scholarship.
examples: Our son is doing well *academically* but struggles to make friends.
The school admits only *academically* gifted students.
*Academically*, it was her best year.

position: end — or before its word (*acceptably safe*)

senses.gloss: Well enough to be accepted; satisfactorily.
examples: The car ran *acceptably* after the repair.
Is the water *acceptably* clean?
Students must perform *acceptably* on the final exam to pass.

position: mid — before the main verb; also end
contrast: *Accidentally* means 'by mistake, without meaning to'. In questions, Russian *случайно* ('do you happen to…') is *by any chance* (*Do you have a pen, by any chance?*), never *accidentally*.

senses.gloss: By mistake; without meaning to.
examples: I *accidentally* deleted the whole file.
She *accidentally* locked herself out of the car.
The fire was started *accidentally* by a cigarette.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Correctly and exactly, without mistakes.
examples: The forecast *accurately* predicted the storm.
Please fill out the form *accurately*.
We can't measure the distance *more accurately* without a laser.

position: end

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you think someone did something wrong.
examples: She looked at me *accusingly*.
“You ate the last cookie,” he said *accusingly*.
The dog stared *accusingly* at its empty bowl.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*acoustically perfect*); end in the 'unplugged' sense
modifies: adjectives and verbs of playing and recording

senses.gloss: In terms of sound.
examples: The new concert hall is *acoustically* excellent.
*Acoustically*, the room was a disaster.

senses.gloss: On instruments that are not electrically amplified.
examples: The band played the last three songs *acoustically*.
She recorded the whole album *acoustically* in her kitchen.

position: mid — before the main verb; also end

senses.gloss: In a busy, energetic way that involves doing things.
examples: We're *actively* looking for a new office.
She's been *actively* involved in the campaign from the start.
Try to take part *more actively* in class discussions.

position: before its word — before adjectives, especially *aware* and *embarrassed*; end with verbs like *feel*

senses.gloss: Very strongly or sharply, of a feeling or a problem.
examples: I was *acutely* aware that everyone was watching me.
She felt the loss *acutely*.
The shortage of nurses is *acutely* felt in rural hospitals.

position: mid — before the verb, especially *refuse*, *deny*, *oppose*
modifies: verbs and participles of refusing and opposing

senses.gloss: Firmly, refusing to change your mind.
examples: He *adamantly* denied taking the money.
The mayor is *adamantly* opposed to the new stadium.
She *adamantly* refused to apologize.

position: end — or before its word (*adequately prepared*)

senses.gloss: Well enough for the purpose.
examples: Were you *adequately* prepared for the interview?
The house wasn't *adequately* heated.
He couldn't explain his decision *adequately*.

position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs; front with a comma

senses.gloss: In terms of management and official procedures.
examples: The two campuses are *administratively* separate.
The case was handled *administratively*, not in court.
*Administratively*, the merger was a nightmare.

position: end — or before its word (*admirably clear*)
form: -ly from *admirable* — stressed on AD, not on the *-mire-* of *admire*

senses.gloss: Very well, in a way that deserves respect.
examples: She handled a difficult situation *admirably*.
The report is *admirably* clear.
The volunteers performed *admirably* under pressure.

position: end

senses.gloss: In a way that shows admiration.
examples: He looked at the painting *admiringly*.
People whistled *admiringly* as the old car drove past.
“You built all this yourself?” she asked *admiringly*.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*adorably clumsy*); end with verbs

senses.gloss: In a sweet, charming way.
examples: The puppy was *adorably* clumsy.
She looked *adorably* confused.
The kids were dressed *adorably* in matching sweaters.

position: end
modifies: verbs of looking, smiling and speaking

senses.gloss: With great love and admiration.
examples: The dog gazed *adoringly* at its owner.
She smiled *adoringly* at her new baby.
He talks *adoringly* about his grandkids.

position: end — mostly after *be*, *cast*, *set* or *leave*

senses.gloss: Floating without being steered or tied; figuratively, without direction or support.
examples: The boat was *adrift* for three days before it was found.
The fishermen were cast *adrift* when their engine failed.
Without a leader, the party has been left *adrift*.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Skillfully and cleverly, especially in a tricky situation.
examples: She *adroitly* changed the subject.
The senator *adroitly* avoided answering the question.
He steered the car *adroitly* through the traffic.

position: end — or before a participle (*advantageously located*)

senses.gloss: In a way that gives an advantage or benefit.
examples: The house is *advantageously* located near the train station.
She invested her savings *advantageously*.
The new rules could work *advantageously* for small businesses.

position: mid — before the verb, especially *affect*; also end

senses.gloss: In a harmful or negative way.
examples: The drought *adversely* affected this year's harvest.
Patients who reacted *adversely* to the drug were removed from the study.
Rising interest rates could *adversely* impact home sales.

position: end — mostly in *I use the word advisedly*
modifies: verbs of choosing and using words
form: -ly from *advised*, with an extra syllable: uhd-VY-zid-lee

senses.gloss: Deliberately, after careful thought, especially about a choice of words.
examples: I use the word “disaster” *advisedly*.
He chose his words *advisedly*.
The term “crisis” is used *advisedly* in this report.

position: before its word — especially in *aesthetically pleasing*; front with a comma

senses.gloss: In terms of beauty or appearance.
examples: The new bridge is both practical and *aesthetically* pleasing.
*Aesthetically*, I prefer the older design.
The furniture was chosen *aesthetically*, not for comfort.

type: place — formal, almost always in *from afar*
position: end — after *from*
modifies: verbs of seeing, coming and admiring

senses.gloss: From or at a great distance.
examples: She had admired him from *afar* for years.
Visitors came from *afar* to see the festival.
From *afar*, the island looked deserted.

position: end
modifies: verbs of talking, smiling and greeting

senses.gloss: In a friendly, easygoing way.
examples: He chatted *affably* with the other guests.
The host greeted us *affably* at the door.
She smiled *affably* and shook everyone's hand.

position: end — or before a participle (*affectionately known as*)

senses.gloss: In a loving, fond way.
examples: She hugged her grandson *affectionately*.
The old professor is *affectionately* known as “Doc.”
He patted the horse *affectionately* on the neck.

position: end

senses.gloss: In a way that means yes.
examples: She nodded *affirmatively*.
Most of the people surveyed answered *affirmatively*.
If you can answer *affirmatively* to all three questions, you qualify.

type: place — mostly in *far afield* and *farther afield*
position: end — after *far* or *farther*
modifies: verbs of traveling, looking and wandering

senses.gloss: Far away from home or from the usual place or topic.
examples: Tourists now come from as far *afield* as Japan.
We had to look farther *afield* for a cheaper apartment.
The discussion wandered far *afield* from the original topic.

type: manner — formal; in speech Americans usually say *start over*
position: end

senses.gloss: Again, in a new way.
examples: After the fire, they had to start *afresh*.
Let's look at the problem *afresh* in the morning.
The committee decided to begin *afresh* with a new plan.

position: end — usually after a time word (*soon after*, *the day after*)
modifies: verbs, with time words before it (*soon*, *long*, *shortly*, *the week*)
contrast: With an object *after* is a preposition (*after lunch*); with a clause it is a conjunction (*after we left*). As an adverb it is most natural with a time word in front (*soon after*); on its own at the end of a sentence, careful writing prefers *afterward* or *later*.

senses.gloss: Later; following something already mentioned.
examples: He left, and she arrived soon *after*.
I saw her the week before the wedding and the day *after*.
They got married and lived happily ever *after*.

position: end — or front (*Afterwards, …*)
contrast: Americans usually say *afterward*, without the *-s*; *afterwards* is the British preference but is also common in the US.

senses.gloss: At a later time; after that.
examples: We went out for ice cream *afterwards*.
*Afterwards*, she couldn't remember what she'd said.
Shortly *afterwards*, the power went out.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: In a hostile, threatening way.
examples: The dog barked *aggressively* at the mail carrier.
He was pulled over for driving *aggressively* on the interstate.

senses.gloss: With great energy and determination to succeed.
examples: The company is *aggressively* expanding into new markets.
The cancer was treated *aggressively* with surgery and chemotherapy.
We need to market the product *more aggressively*.

position: before its word — before adjectives and adverbs, especially *slow* and *close*

senses.gloss: To a painfully frustrating degree.
examples: The line moved *agonizingly* slowly.
They came *agonizingly* close to winning the title.
The wait for the test results was *agonizingly* long.

position: before its word — especially in *agreeably surprised*; end with verbs

senses.gloss: In a pleasant way.
examples: I was *agreeably* surprised by the food.
The evening passed *agreeably* with good wine and conversation.
The weather was *agreeably* mild for March.

position: end
modifies: verbs of moving and passing time

senses.gloss: Without a purpose or direction.
examples: We wandered *aimlessly* around the mall.
He spent the summer drifting *aimlessly* from job to job.
She was flipping *aimlessly* through the channels.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: In a light, careless way, as if something does not matter.
examples: “Oh, it's nothing,” she said *airily*.
He waved *airily* at the pile of bills.
The governor *airily* dismissed the report.

position: after its word — after *arms*, *legs* or *elbows*
modifies: the nouns *arms*, *legs* and *elbows* in fixed phrases

senses.gloss: With hands on the hips and elbows pointing out; of legs, spread out at odd angles.
examples: She stood in the doorway with arms *akimbo*.
The kids sprawled on the couch, legs *akimbo*.
He waited by the car, arms *akimbo*, looking annoyed.

position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs of change; front as a comment (*Alarmingly, …*)
modifies: adjectives, verbs of change, and whole sentences

senses.gloss: To a worrying degree; in a way that causes alarm.
examples: Crime rates have risen *alarmingly* in the past year.
The river was *alarmingly* high after the storm.
*Alarmingly*, nobody at the plant noticed the leak.

position: end
form: from Italian *al fresco* 'in the fresh air'; also written *al fresco*

senses.gloss: Outdoors, especially of eating a meal.
examples: In summer we like to eat *alfresco* on the patio.
The restaurant lets you dine *alfresco* by the river.
Lunch was served *alfresco* under the trees.

position: end

senses.gloss: By using algebra.
examples: Solve the equation *algebraically*, then check your answer on a graph.
The rule can be expressed *algebraically* in one line.
Show *algebraically* that the two expressions are equal.

position: end

senses.gloss: High up in the air; upward.
examples: The winner held the trophy *aloft*.
Hot air keeps the balloon *aloft*.
The pilot stayed *aloft* for nine hours.

position: end
contrast: With an object *alongside* is a preposition (*parked alongside the curb*, *work alongside experts*); without one it is an adverb.

senses.gloss: Next to someone or something, side by side.
examples: A police car pulled up *alongside*.
The boat came *alongside*, and a man threw us a rope.
She ran ahead, and her dog trotted *alongside*.

position: end
modifies: verbs of reading, thinking, laughing and wondering
contrast: *Aloud* means 'so others can hear' (вслух), not 'in a loud voice' (громко, *loudly*): *read aloud*, but *talk loudly*. *Out loud* means the same as *aloud* and is more common in speech.

senses.gloss: In a voice that other people can hear; not silently.
examples: The teacher asked me to read the poem *aloud*.
Sorry, I was just thinking *aloud*.
She laughed *aloud* at the joke.

position: end

senses.gloss: In the order of the letters of the alphabet.
examples: The files are arranged *alphabetically* by last name.
List the countries *alphabetically*.
The books on this shelf are sorted *alphabetically* by author.

position: end
modifies: verbs; a whole statement in the 'certainly' sense
form: an informal one-word spelling of *all right*
contrast: Many teachers and editors still mark *alright* as wrong, so write *all right* in formal work. In *Are you alright?* it is an adjective, and in *Alright, let's go* it is a reply word — neither is the adverb.

senses.gloss: Well enough; satisfactorily.
examples: The interview went *alright*, I think.
Is the new printer working *alright*?

senses.gloss: Certainly; without any doubt, placed after the statement for emphasis.
examples: That's him *alright* — I'd know that laugh anywhere.
It's cold out there *alright*.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*alternately funny and sad*); end or mid with verbs
modifies: pairs of adjectives or verbs, and verbs
contrast: *Alternately* means 'taking turns, first one and then the other'; *alternatively* means 'as another option' (как вариант). Americans sometimes use *alternately* for 'as another option', but careful writers keep them apart.

senses.gloss: One after the other, again and again.
examples: The movie is *alternately* funny and sad.
She works *alternately* in Boston and New York.
Add the flour and the milk *alternately*, a little at a time.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*not altogether sure*); end with verbs (*stop altogether*); front for 'in total' and 'on the whole'
modifies: adjectives, verbs, amounts, and whole sentences
contrast: *Altogether* (one word) is 'completely' or 'in total'; *all together* (two words) is 'everyone in one place or at the same time' (*We were all together at Christmas*).

senses.gloss: Completely; entirely.
examples: He stopped drinking *altogether*.
I'm not *altogether* sure she's right.
The idea was *altogether* new to me.

senses.gloss: In total; counting everything.
examples: That comes to $45 *altogether*.
*Altogether*, about 200 people showed up.

senses.gloss: On the whole; considering everything.
examples: The weather was bad, but *altogether* it was a good trip.
*Altogether*, I'd say the meeting went well.

position: end — or mid, before the verb
modifies: verbs of acting, giving and helping

senses.gloss: Unselfishly, for the good of others rather than yourself.
examples: Most volunteers act *altruistically*, not for the résumé.
She *altruistically* gave her bonus to the youngest workers.
Nobody believed the company was behaving *altruistically*.

position: end — or before a participle (*amateurishly made*)

senses.gloss: Without skill, like someone who is not a professional.
examples: The website looked *amateurishly* designed.
The robbery was *amateurishly* planned.
The play was performed *amateurishly*, but everyone had fun.

position: end — or before a participle (*ambiguously worded*)

senses.gloss: In a way that can be understood in more than one way.
examples: The contract was *ambiguously* worded.
She answered *ambiguously*, so nobody knew what she meant.
The law is written so *ambiguously* that lawyers still argue about it.

position: end — or before a participle (*ambitiously titled*)

senses.gloss: In a way that aims for something big or difficult.
examples: The city has *ambitiously* planned a new light rail system.
The book is *ambitiously* titled “Everything You Need to Know.”
They started *ambitiously* but ran out of money within a year.

position: end
modifies: verbs of talking, smiling and getting along
contrast: *Amiably* describes a friendly manner; *amicably* describes ending a dispute or relationship without a fight (*split up amicably*).

senses.gloss: In a pleasant, friendly way.
examples: The two men chatted *amiably* over coffee.
He smiled *amiably* and offered to help.
The neighbors got along *amiably* for years.

position: end
contrast: *Amicably* is about settling or ending something without a fight; *amiably* is simply 'in a friendly manner' (*chat amiably*).

senses.gloss: Without arguing or fighting; on friendly terms.
examples: The dispute was settled *amicably* out of court.
They divorced *amicably* and are still friends.
The band split up *amicably* after ten years.

position: end — right after *run*

senses.gloss: Wildly and out of control, in *run amok*.
examples: The kids ran *amok* while the teacher was out of the room.
Rumors ran *amok* on social media.
A bull ran *amok* through the streets of the town.

position: before its word — before participles and verbs (*amply rewarded*, *amply demonstrate*)

senses.gloss: More than enough; fully.
examples: Her hard work was *amply* rewarded.
The results *amply* demonstrate the need for change.
The kitchen is *amply* stocked for the weekend.

position: end — or before a participle (*amusingly written*); front as a comment (*Amusingly, …*)

senses.gloss: In a funny, entertaining way.
examples: He told the story *amusingly*, doing all the voices.
The book is *amusingly* written.
*Amusingly*, the fire station's own alarm didn't work.

position: end — or front as a linker (*Analogously, …*)

senses.gloss: In a similar way; by comparison with a case already mentioned.
examples: The second equation can be solved *analogously*.
*Analogously*, a city's roads work like the blood vessels in a body.
The new rules apply *analogously* to part-time employees.

position: end
modifies: verbs of thinking, approaching and solving

senses.gloss: By careful, logical analysis.
examples: Try to think about the problem *analytically*.
She approaches every big decision *analytically*.
The equation can't be solved *analytically*, only by computer.

position: before its word — before adjectives (*anatomically correct*); front with a comma

senses.gloss: In terms of the structure of the body.
examples: The model of the heart is *anatomically* correct.
The two species are *anatomically* very similar.
*Anatomically*, humans aren't built for sitting all day.

position: end

senses.gloss: Again, often in a new or different way.
examples: After the divorce, she moved to Denver to start life *anew*.
The debate over gun laws began *anew* after the shooting.
Every spring the garden comes to life *anew*.

position: end
modifies: verbs of smiling, singing and looking

senses.gloss: Sweetly and innocently, like an angel.
examples: The baby smiled *angelically* at us.
The children's choir sang *angelically*.
She looked up *angelically*, as if she hadn't eaten the cake.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: In an angry way.
examples: “Get out!” he shouted *angrily*.
She *angrily* slammed the door.
Protesters reacted *angrily* to the decision.

position: end

senses.gloss: In a lively, excited way.
examples: They were talking *animatedly* about the game.
She gestured *animatedly* as she told the story.
The kids chattered *animatedly* on the bus.

position: before its word — before adjectives; front as a comment (*Annoyingly, …*)

senses.gloss: In a way that annoys you; to an annoying degree.
examples: The song was *annoyingly* catchy.
*Annoyingly*, the store closed five minutes before we got there.
He's *annoyingly* good at every sport.

position: end

senses.gloss: Without giving your name.
examples: The money was donated *anonymously*.
You can report the problem *anonymously*.
The letter was sent *anonymously* to the newspaper.

position: end — or mid, before the verb
modifies: verbs of waiting, watching and looking

senses.gloss: In a worried, nervous way.
examples: She looked *anxiously* at the clock.
Parents waited *anxiously* for news of the missing hikers.

senses.gloss: Eagerly, while waiting for something you want.
examples: Fans are *anxiously* awaiting the band's new album.
The kids have been *anxiously* counting the days until summer.

position: end
contrast: *Anyplace* is informal American English for *anywhere*; use *anywhere* in formal writing. As with *anywhere*, a negative sentence gives the Russian *нигде*.

senses.gloss: In or to any place; anywhere.
examples: You can sit *anyplace* you like.
I can't find my glasses *anyplace*.
Is there *anyplace* around here that's open this late?

position: front or end
contrast: *Anyways* belongs to informal American speech; in writing, and in anything formal, use *anyway*.

senses.gloss: Anyway: despite that, or to change or return to a topic.
examples: *Anyways*, where was I?
It was raining, but we went *anyways*.
*Anyways*, I have to go — talk to you later.

type: manner — formal, common in news writing
position: end — usually after *continue*, *proceed* or *grow*

senses.gloss: Quickly; at a fast pace.
examples: Work on the new stadium continues *apace*.
Technology is advancing *apace*.
Construction proceeded *apace* despite the protests.

position: after its word — after a price, number or amount

senses.gloss: For each one; each.
examples: The tickets cost $20 *apiece*.
The kids got two cookies *apiece*.
The houses sold for over a million dollars *apiece*.

position: end
modifies: verbs of speaking, smiling and shrugging

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you are sorry.
examples: “I'm so sorry I'm late,” she said *apologetically*.
He smiled *apologetically* and moved his bag off the seat.
The waiter shrugged *apologetically*.

position: before its word — before adjectives; end with verbs

senses.gloss: Shockingly badly; to a shocking degree.
examples: The prisoners were treated *appallingly*.
The hospital was *appallingly* dirty.
His spelling is *appallingly* bad for a journalist.

position: before its word — before adjectives; end in the 'pleading' sense
modifies: adjectives, participles, and verbs of looking

senses.gloss: In an attractive or pleasing way.
examples: The idea is *appealingly* simple.
The dishes were *appealingly* arranged on the table.

senses.gloss: In a pleading way, asking for help or sympathy.
examples: The puppy looked up at me *appealingly*.
She glanced *appealingly* at her father.

position: before its word — before adjectives and comparatives; end or mid with verbs of change
modifies: adjectives, comparatives, and verbs of change

senses.gloss: Enough to be noticed or measured.
examples: Prices haven't changed *appreciably* in a year.
The new medicine didn't *appreciably* improve her condition.
The second model is *appreciably* lighter.

position: end
modifies: verbs of reacting, looking and tasting

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you enjoy or are grateful for something.
examples: The audience laughed *appreciatively*.
He sniffed the wine *appreciatively*.
She nodded *appreciatively* when I finished explaining.

position: end
modifies: verbs of looking, waiting and approaching

senses.gloss: In a worried way, fearing something bad may happen.
examples: She looked *apprehensively* at the dark water.
He opened the envelope *apprehensively*.
The students waited *apprehensively* for their grades.

position: end — or before its word (*appropriately dressed*); front as a comment (*Appropriately, …*)

senses.gloss: In a way that is suitable or right for the situation.
examples: Please dress *appropriately* for the interview.
The hotel is *appropriately* named Ocean View.
Staff didn't respond *appropriately* to the complaint.

position: end
modifies: verbs of nodding, smiling and speaking

senses.gloss: In a way that shows you think something is good.
examples: Her father nodded *approvingly*.
The crowd murmured *approvingly*.
He spoke *approvingly* of the new policy.

type: degree — an approximator, more formal than *about* or *around*
position: before its word — before numbers, amounts and times

senses.gloss: A little more or less than; roughly.
examples: The flight takes *approximately* four hours.
*Approximately* 30 percent of voters are still undecided.
The two paintings were done at *approximately* the same time.

position: before its word — especially before *named*, *described* and *put*
modifies: participles and verbs of naming and describing

senses.gloss: In a way that fits very well.
examples: The town is *aptly* named Mosquito Creek.
As one critic *aptly* put it, the movie is all style and no story.
Her boss *aptly* described the plan as a gamble.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: Without a reason or system; by chance or personal whim.
examples: The winners were chosen *arbitrarily*.
The rules seem to be enforced *arbitrarily*.
He *arbitrarily* decided to cancel the trip.

position: before its word — before adjectives; front with a comma

senses.gloss: In terms of architecture or the design of buildings.
examples: The building is *architecturally* significant.
*Architecturally*, the city is a mix of old and new.
It's one of the most *architecturally* interesting neighborhoods in Chicago.

position: mid — before the verb; also end
modifies: verbs of supporting, believing and loving

senses.gloss: With strong feeling or enthusiasm.
examples: She *ardently* supports animal rights.
He was *ardently* in love with her.
They argued *ardently* for a change in the law.

position: end — or mid, before the verb

senses.gloss: In a proud way that shows you think you are better than others.
examples: He *arrogantly* assumed he would win.
She dismissed our concerns *arrogantly*.
The CEO behaved *arrogantly* toward his staff.

position: end — or before a participle (*artfully arranged*)

senses.gloss: With skill and good taste.
examples: The flowers were *artfully* arranged in a glass vase.
The film *artfully* mixes comedy and tragedy.

senses.gloss: In a clever, slightly sly way.
examples: She *artfully* avoided answering the question.
The report *artfully* hides how much money was lost.

position: end
modifies: verbs of speaking, writing and explaining

senses.gloss: Clearly and effectively, in well-chosen words.
examples: She spoke *articulately* about her experience.
He explained the problem calmly and *articulately*.
Few politicians argue as *articulately* as she does.

position: before its word — before adjectives and participles (*artificially sweetened*); end with verbs

senses.gloss: Not naturally; made or done by people.
examples: The drink is *artificially* sweetened.
Prices are being kept *artificially* high.
The lake was created *artificially* in the 1930s.

ru: художественно, артистично; с художественной точки зрения
position: end — or before its word (*artistically gifted*); front as a viewpoint (*Artistically, …*)
modifies: verbs, participles, adjectives, and whole sentences

senses.gloss: In an artistic way, or in terms of art.
examples: The food was *artistically* arranged on the plate.
Their daughter is very *artistically* gifted.
*Artistically*, the film is a triumph, but it lost money.

position: end
form: abbreviation of *as soon as possible*; said letter by letter or as one word, AY-sap

senses.gloss: As soon as possible.
examples: Please call me back *ASAP*.
I need those reports *ASAP*.
Get here *ASAP* — the meeting's about to start.

position: end

senses.gloss: Without sex, especially of reproduction in plants and simple organisms.
examples: Some plants reproduce *asexually*.
Bacteria multiply *asexually* by splitting in two.
Starfish can reproduce both sexually and *asexually*.

position: end — after *look* or *view*

senses.gloss: With suspicion or disapproval.
examples: The neighbors looked *askance* at the new family.
Many doctors still view the treatment *askance*.
My parents looked *askance* at my plan to quit college.
